name: Sam Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the returns and packing line at a big online clothing warehouse, the one by the old brickworks on Canal Road. On a Monday after a sale we get maybe 9,000 parcels back, and my team of eleven opens them, checks for make-up stains and missing tags, and decides what goes back on the shelf. I'm the one people call when the scanner says a jacket doesn't exist. I like that it's a puzzle every day, even if the puzzles are mostly other people's mess.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Leo, who's in his last year training as a nurse, so right now it's mostly my wage paying the rent. We've got maybe two weeks of bills saved, and pay here is lower than the parcel hubs in the city. There's one other warehouse in town and it's hiring less than us. Once Leo qualifies next September, things should loosen up a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. At work I'd tell the team that the chatbots will help with the paperwork, but nobody is going to replace the person who can smell perfume on a returned shirt. Online I'd stay quiet, because everyone shouting about AI gets on my nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job stays and so does my squeeze. The next year is about getting to Leo's first nurse's payslip without the car failing its test. If nothing changes with AI, the only change I care about is that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the line and keep using the translation app with the new starters, since it actually works. I'd ask my manager, Ruth, about the team-lead pay band I was half promised last year. And I'd go to the next workers' forum meeting, because the heating in the returns area has been broken since October.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little bit stuck. It's like waiting at a bus stop when you can see the bus at the end of the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the translation app works. How did you start using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of the new lads, Karim, only had a bit of English, and I was miming instructions like a clown. A friend on days showed me the app, I tried it for a week, and now I use it every shift. I don't trust it for anything about safety though; for that I get a person who speaks his language.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the car did fail its test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be cycling eleven kilometres each way in the dark, which I've done before. I'd ask my brother for a loan before I'd use a credit card. It's not a disaster, it's just tiring, and I'd be grumpy for a month.

say: The chatbots will help with **paperwork**, but nobody replaces a person who checks returns by hand.
I'd keep quiet online, because the **AI shouting** gets on my nerves.
think: My job stays, and so does the **money squeeze** until Leo qualifies.
The only change that matters to me is **Leo's first payslip** next September.
do: Ask Ruth about the **team-lead pay band** promised last year.
Raise the **broken heating** at the next workers' forum.
Keep using the **translation app** with new starters.
feel: **Mostly fine** but a little stuck, like waiting for a bus he can already see.
S0.quote: Nobody is going to replace the person who can smell perfume on a returned shirt.
fieldNote: His job feels safe, but **two weeks of savings** keep the margin thin until his partner qualifies.
Uses AI only where it has **proven itself**, and never for safety.
Turns small problems into **collective issues**, like the heating, through the workers' forum.

steps.text: Ask Ruth for the promised team-lead pay band
Raise the broken heating in returns at the workers' forum
Ask his brother for a loan if the car fails its test

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and we should make sure the gains get shared. At work I'd tell people the customer-service lot will feel it first, not us. Online I'd share stuff about a shorter working week, because that's one way to spread the work around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it hits the office upstairs before it hits me. The people who answer customer emails about refunds would be cut, and some of their checking work might land on my line through a screen. Robots for returns are slow to come, because every returned parcel is a different mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the first company system looks like and then learn it properly once I'd watched it work for a month. I'd ask to be on whatever group tests it, because the lead who knows the new system keeps their job. And I'd join the union properly instead of just going to the forum, since there'd finally be something to bargain about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit of interest. I like puzzles, and a new system is a puzzle, as long as it doesn't come with a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who upstairs would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who answers refund emails, sits with us at lunch and has two kids. She already says the bot does half her replies. If her team shrinks, I'd want the company to offer people like Priya a spot on the floor before hiring outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a month before learning it. Isn't that risky if others jump in first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I've seen three systems come and go here, and the first month is always a mess. I'd rather be the one who knows how it really works than the one who clicked first. Ruth knows I pick things up quickly once they settle.

say: The **gains should be shared**, maybe through a shorter working week.
The **customer-service team** will feel it before the warehouse floor does.
think: Refund-email jobs upstairs shrink, and some **checking work** lands on my line.
Robots for returns come **slowly**, because every returned parcel is a different mess.
do: Join the **union** properly instead of only going to the forum.
Ask to join the **test group** for the new returns system.
Learn the system **after a month** of watching it settle.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some curiosity, as long as a new system doesn't bring a pay cut.
S1.quote: I've seen three systems come and go here, and the first month is always a mess.
fieldNote: He reads the disruption accurately: **office jobs** first, returns work later.
His steadiness is **deliberate**: he waits a month, then learns deeply.
Worried for colleagues like **Priya** more than for himself.

steps.text: Join the union instead of only going to the workers' forum
Volunteer for the test group on the new returns system
Run the returns line as usual while the system settles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in hard, with a wage guarantee or something, because markets won't sort it in two years. At work I'd try to keep people calm, because panic makes people quit before they have to. Online I'd share stuff about a universal basic income, meaning a regular payment everyone gets from the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd have about five years before a robot can do what my team does. In 2028 the thinking jobs around me vanish, the planners and the refund people, and then by 2031 the robots come for the hands. My partner Leo's nursing job is the one thing in our house that might hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From now I'd save every spare bit, even 30 a week, and stop thinking about a bigger flat. I'd look at the hospital's porter and logistics jobs, because hospitals need people and Leo would be there anyway. And I'd go to every union meeting and push for redundancy pay that actually covers a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. Picturing Leo paying all the bills while I look for work makes my stomach turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would that picture make your stomach turn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been the one carrying us while Leo studies, and I'm proud of that. Swapping round wouldn't be fair on Leo after all those placements. I know couples do it, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would hospital logistics be safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not forever. But a hospital moves slower than an online clothing company, and there'd be rules about patients that slow robots down. I'd be buying time, and right now time is what I'd need.

say: Governments should step in with a **wage guarantee**, because markets won't sort this in two years.
I'd keep people **calm at work** so nobody quits before they have to.
think: I'd have about **five years** before robots can do my team's work.
Leo's **nursing job** might be the one income in our house that holds.
do: Save **30 a week** and drop the idea of a bigger flat.
Apply for **hospital logistics** or porter jobs near Leo's work.
Push the union for **a year's redundancy** pay.
feel: **Alarmed**, and sick at the thought of Leo paying all the bills.
S2.quote: My partner Leo's nursing job is the one thing in our house that might hold.
fieldNote: He maps the **2028 and 2031 dates** clearly onto the office and the floor.
Pride in being the **main earner** shapes his fear more than the job itself.
Picks a **hospital job** to buy time, knowing it isn't safe forever.

steps.text: Save 30 a week and drop plans for a bigger flat
Apply for hospital porter and logistics jobs near Leo's work
Push the union for redundancy pay covering a full year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and we should treat it like one. At work I'd tell people to get any certificate the company will pay for, now. Online I'd share stuff about getting the state to fund retraining before it's urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have till about 2034, and by then Leo would be a few years into nursing. That changes it a lot. I'd be the one changing careers while the other one is steady, which is how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for the engineering maintenance course they run for a few people a year, since someone has to fix the robots for a while. I'd wait to see which robot makers win before betting on one. And I'd start saving properly once Leo's pay comes in, maybe 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but with a plan. I can picture next year, which I couldn't in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't robot maintenance also at risk once the robots are good enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, eventually. But somebody has to oil the robots, swap the batteries and explain to my manager why one keeps crashing into the racking. That's ten years of work, maybe, and I'd be 37 by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the union a few times. What would you want it to win in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A training budget written into the contract, for every person, not just the favourites. And a promise that the first lay-offs are voluntary, with decent money. I'd stand in the car park with a clipboard for that.

say: **Five years** is a warning, so get any certificate the company will pay for now.
The state should fund **retraining** before it's urgent.
think: I'd have until about **2034**, while Leo is settled in nursing.
One of us changing careers while the other is **steady** feels manageable.
do: Apply for the company's **maintenance course** for robot technicians.
Save **200 a month** once Leo's nursing pay starts.
Campaign for a **training budget** in every contract.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan; he can picture next year this time.
S3.quote: Somebody has to oil the robots, swap the batteries and explain to my manager why one keeps crashing into the racking.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **two-stage plan** tied to Leo's income.
Accepts robot maintenance is **temporary**, but values a decade.
His union demands are **specific**: training budgets and voluntary lay-offs first.

steps.text: Apply for the company's robot maintenance course
Save 200 a month once Leo's nursing pay starts
Collect signatures for a training budget in every contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, if we don't waste it. At work I'd say learn something now while it's calm. Online I'd probably not say much; I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years would let me get properly qualified in something, maybe as an electrician. Leo and I could even start thinking about a mortgage. But it's the same ending, so I wouldn't relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the returns line and start an evening electrical course at the college in year two, once Leo's pay settles things. I'd try the AI tools the college uses so I'm not behind. And I'd stay in the union, because ten years of good contracts matters too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. Like knowing the rent will go up next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Tomas is an electrician, and he's never short of work. Robots will need wiring, houses will need wiring, and it's a trade with a licence. I'd be slower to learn than a 17-year-old, but I'm good with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo about a mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's wait two years and see if I can get on the course. If I'm in, we look at small flats near the hospital. If not, we keep renting and I keep my head down.

say: **Ten years** is plenty, if we don't waste it.
People should **learn something now** while things are calm.
think: Ten years would let me get properly qualified as an **electrician**.
It's the **same ending**, so I wouldn't relax completely.
do: Start an **evening electrical course** in year two.
Try the **AI tools** the college uses so he isn't behind.
Stay in the **union** for better contracts in the meantime.
feel: **Uneasy**, in a normal way, like knowing rent will rise next year.
S4.quote: My uncle Tomas is an electrician, and he's never short of work.
fieldNote: With ten years, he plans a **licensed trade** through family example.
A **mortgage** becomes thinkable only in this picture.
Still steady, not eager: he'd start the course in **year two**, not now.

steps.text: Start an evening electrical course at the college in year two
Use the college's AI tools to keep up in class
Wait two years before looking at small flats with Leo

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands while Leo is still training and I'm the only wage. What would help is a wage guarantee while people retrain, and the company paying for courses before the robots come, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who are new to the country. A screen in English is a wall for half my team, and nobody plans for that. They're good workers, and they'd be the first ones lost.

headlineQuote: A screen in English is a wall for half my team, and nobody plans for that.
portrait: Sam, 27, runs a **returns line** at an online clothing warehouse and is the main earner at home.
His partner Leo is **training as a nurse**, and their savings cover about two weeks.
He adopts tech once it's **proven**, like the translation app, and waits out first-month chaos.
He is uneasy in mild pictures, **alarmed** at 2028, and plans a trade with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving while he is the only wage in the household.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage guarantee** during retraining, and company-paid courses before robots arrive.
